text.p: Debt-laden Italian flag carrier Alitalia is hoping to reach breakeven point this year after chalking up losses for the ninth year in a row in 1996, financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said on Saturday.

An Alitalia report envisaged a 1997 result "before extraordinary components and taxes, of around breakeven," Il Sole said, adding the airline expected the net result to include "the benefits of significant capital gains" through divestments.

Alitalia late on Friday said it posted a consolidated loss of 1.203 trillion lire ($719 million) after accounting for restructuring costs of 901 billion lire. This compared with a 1995 group loss of 85.9 billion lire.
The parent loss totalled 1.217 trillion last year after a profit in 1995 of 1.3 trillion due to capital gains.
The airline also appointed three trade unionists to the board in line with an accord reached with labour leaders last year on a plan to rescue the floundering airline.
The agreement included reserving up to 30 percent of Alitalia's capital for employees in exchanged for 2,000 job cuts from the 17,000-strong workforce.
The three trade unionists, Augusto Angioletti, Guido Abbadessa and Giuseppe Surrenti, replace three directors from Italian state industrial holding IRI.

Angioletti told La Repubblica newspaper the labour leaders would develop a role which would "contribute to taking Alitalia back to financial health through privatisation and new alliances, which are indispensable for recovering the competitiveness needed in a new free market."
The troubled airline, which turned 50 years old in early May, has been battling to get the rescue plan off the ground and return to profit.

Its sales revenue grew 3.3 percent in 1996 to 7.81 trillion lire and net financial indebtedness fell to 2.34 trillion lire from 3.42 trillion previously. Total indebtedness fell 829 billion to 3.831 trillion.

Italy requested European Union permission last year for a capital injection worth 3.3 trillion lire into Alitalia to prepare it for eventual privatisation, although the carrier's managing director Domenico Cempella said recently the EU Commission had requested a reduction to 2.8 trillion.
Italy and the EU Commission are still trying to iron differences over the plan and a final decision is not expected before the end of June.
